summaries.example: Imagine someone explaining a difficult book by breaking it into small parts, comparing it with other books, and saving ideas that might otherwise be lost. Simplicius did something like this with Aristotle’s writings. He also tried to show how Aristotle and Plato could fit together, even when their words seemed different.
summaries.summary: Simplicius was a philosopher and careful reader of ancient Greek thought. He explained works by Aristotle and Epictetus, while bringing in Plato and many earlier philosophers. He often looked for a deeper agreement among these thinkers instead of treating every difference in wording as a real disagreement. Still, he was not simply copying them: he sometimes criticized Aristotle and developed his own Neoplatonic ideas. His books are especially valuable because they preserve pieces of older philosophy that might otherwise have disappeared. They also show that, for Simplicius, studying nature and the human soul could be part of a spiritual path.
key_ideas: Simplicius was a Greek-speaking philosopher from Cilicia who lived about 480–560 CE.
He wrote detailed explanations of Aristotle and Epictetus.
He tried to connect the ideas of Plato, Aristotle, and older Greek philosophers.
His writings saved information from many earlier thinkers whose own works no longer survive.
His commentaries were also spiritual works, not only school-like explanations.
summaries.why_it_matters: Simplicius shows how ideas can travel through time. A careful reader may preserve old knowledge, compare different thinkers, and add a new interpretation. His works help modern scholars learn about ancient philosophy, including writings that are now lost. They also remind us that philosophy can be both an effort to understand arguments and a way of thinking about how a person should live.

important_terms.definition: A person who explains a difficult book or idea, often by discussing each part carefully.
A later form of Platonism that joined Plato’s ideas with religious and spiritual ideas.
A way of reading two thinkers as mostly agreeing, or as adding useful pieces to one larger view.
A very old Greek philosopher whose writings Simplicius helped preserve by discussing and quoting them.

questions_to_think_about: Can two people disagree about words but still agree about an important idea?
Why is it useful to save old arguments and explanations?
Should an explainer point out mistakes in a writer they admire?
How might someone’s religious beliefs affect the way they read philosophy?

summaries.example: Suppose a student is comparing two scientific theories that use different vocabulary. One theory describes what can be observed, while the other explains deeper principles. The student might argue that the theories are compatible in some respects, but not identical. Simplicius approached Plato and Aristotle in a related way: he often treated Aristotle as working from nature and Plato as emphasizing intelligible or theological principles, then sought a larger system in which their approaches could complement one another.
summaries.summary: Simplicius of Cilicia was a late-ancient Neoplatonist whose commentaries became an unusually rich record of earlier Greek philosophy. Educated in Alexandria and Athens, he worked within a tradition shaped by figures such as Proclus, Iamblichus, and Damascius, while drawing especially heavily on Alexander of Aphrodisias. His surviving commentaries explain Aristotle’s Categories, Physics, and On the Heavens, as well as Epictetus’ Handbook; the attribution of a commentary on On the Soul is contested. Simplicius’ method combines close reading, discussions of terminology, historical reports, digressions, and arguments about philosophical puzzles. He urges interpreters to understand an author’s whole body of work and to distinguish surface wording from intended meaning. This allows him to argue that Plato and Aristotle are harmonious in many respects, though not necessarily identical. His project is also religious and spiritual: philosophy, theology, and the purification or ascent of the soul belong together. His polemics against the Christian Platonist John Philoponus occur within wider disputes about the ancient Greek tradition, including the question of whether the cosmos was created in time. Simplicius’ importance therefore lies both in his own philosophical agenda and in his preservation of otherwise lost sources.
key_ideas: Simplicius, who came from Cilicia and studied in Alexandria and Athens, became one of the most important Neoplatonic interpreters of Aristotle.
His surviving works include commentaries on Epictetus’ Handbook and Aristotle’s Categories, Physics, and On the Heavens; the authorship of a commentary on On the Soul remains disputed.
He presents the ideal commentator as knowledgeable, fair, attentive to an author’s language, and willing to pursue truth rather than defend a school blindly.
He frequently interprets Aristotle as compatible with Plato and older Greek traditions, while still criticizing Aristotle in some cases.
Alexander of Aphrodisias strongly influenced Simplicius, but Simplicius objected to Alexander’s tendency to oppose Aristotle to Plato.
The commentaries preserve extensive material from earlier thinkers and later influenced Byzantine, Arabic, Latin, and Renaissance readers.
summaries.why_it_matters: Simplicius illustrates that commentary is not passive repetition. A commentator selects, organizes, compares, criticizes, and gives older arguments a new philosophical purpose. His works are indispensable evidence for Presocratic, Platonic, and Peripatetic traditions, yet they must be read with attention to his Neoplatonic aims. Studying him also clarifies how philosophical traditions respond to disagreement: by rejecting an opponent, distinguishing levels of meaning, or constructing a broader system in which positions can coexist. His later influence shows how ancient texts continued to shape medieval, Arabic, Byzantine, and Renaissance philosophy.

important_terms.definition: A detailed explanation of a text, usually organized by smaller passages and attentive to both arguments and wording.
A late ancient philosophical tradition that interpreted Aristotle through a Platonic framework and connected philosophy with theology and spiritual practice.
An interpretation that treats apparently conflicting views as compatible, complementary, or parts of one larger system; it need not claim that the views are identical.
The philosophical tradition associated with Aristotle and his successors, especially the study of nature, logic, and the interpretation of Aristotle’s works.
A preliminary account of a text’s aim, usefulness, authenticity, structure, and place within a philosophical curriculum or order of reading.
A short, relatively independent discussion inserted into a commentary rather than following the main passage-by-passage explanation.
A method that identifies problems or puzzles and then develops possible answers to them.
The practice of interpreting a philosophical text as contributing to ethical, religious, or spiritual transformation, not merely to information.

questions_to_think_about: When does explaining away a contradiction become an unfair interpretation?
Can a commentator be impartial toward one philosopher while favoring another?
What is gained, and what might be lost, when Aristotle is read through a Platonic framework?
Why might a technical work on physics also be treated as spiritually meaningful?
Is preserving an old argument different from agreeing with it?

summaries.example: Think of two friends describing the same game. One focuses on the visible moves and rules; the other focuses on the game’s deeper meaning and purpose. Their descriptions may sound different without being completely opposed. Simplicius used a similar strategy with Aristotle and Plato. He often said that Aristotle paid close attention to nature and ordinary language, while Plato reached toward deeper intellectual or divine principles. Simplicius then looked for ways those approaches could belong together.
summaries.summary: Simplicius was a philosopher from Cilicia who lived during late antiquity, a period when Greek philosophical traditions faced a Christian political and religious environment. He studied in Alexandria and Athens and became a major Neoplatonic interpreter of Aristotle. Four commentaries survive with clear attribution: works on Epictetus’ Handbook and Aristotle’s Categories, Physics, and On the Heavens. A fifth work on On the Soul may or may not be his. Simplicius did more than summarize Aristotle. He used earlier commentaries, especially those of Alexander of Aphrodisias, and brought together material from Plato, Aristotle, and even older Greek thinkers. He thought a strong interpreter should know the author’s entire system, understand the author’s language, and be fair. Yet his fairness had limits: he often criticized Aristotle but does not appear to criticize Plato. His main interpretive goal was harmony. When Aristotle seemed to disagree with Plato, Simplicius could argue that the disagreement concerned wording, a surface meaning, or different but compatible approaches. His commentaries also include religious and spiritual themes, presenting philosophical study as connected with the soul’s improvement. Because he quoted and discussed many earlier writers, his works became an important source for ideas that no longer survive elsewhere.
key_ideas: Simplicius lived in late antiquity and learned from important Neoplatonic teachers in Alexandria and Athens.
He explained Aristotle and Epictetus in large, carefully organized commentaries.
He believed a good commentator should understand an author deeply, know the author’s language, and remain fair rather than blindly defend a favorite thinker.
He usually tried to reconcile Plato and Aristotle, but this meant compatibility or cooperation, not that they held exactly the same opinions.
He relied greatly on Alexander of Aphrodisias while criticizing Alexander for treating Aristotle as an opponent of Plato.
His commentaries preserved many ideas and passages from earlier philosophers and later influenced readers in several cultures.
summaries.why_it_matters: Simplicius helps us see how philosophical traditions are preserved and reshaped. His commentaries are historical sources, but they are also arguments for a particular view: that the ancient Greek tradition forms a coherent body of wisdom and that Plato and Aristotle can often be read together. This makes his work useful in two ways. It tells us about earlier philosophers, and it shows how an interpreter’s own beliefs influence what they notice, defend, and connect.

important_terms.definition: Someone who explains a difficult text by examining its parts, language, arguments, and larger purpose.
A philosophical movement that combined Plato’s thought with later interpretations and connected philosophy with theology and the soul’s improvement.
The idea that different thinkers can be compatible or complementary even when they do not say exactly the same thing.
The school and tradition connected with Aristotle, including his later interpreters and the study of his works.
An inserted discussion that temporarily leaves the main explanation to explore a related philosophical question.
A list or report of earlier philosophical opinions, often preserved for historical study.
A set of opening questions about a text’s purpose, usefulness, authorship, organization, and place in a course of study.

questions_to_think_about: Why might someone search for agreement between thinkers instead of emphasizing their disagreements?
Can a person be a loyal follower of Plato and still criticize Aristotle?
How does saving another philosopher’s ideas change the way we understand history?
What clues would show that a commentary has a spiritual purpose as well as an academic one?
